entries.objective: Understand why an aperiodic server is needed in a real-time system with mixed periodic and aperiodic tasks, and understand the core idea of the Improved Priority Exchange (IPE) server.
entries.prompt: Through a step-by-step question-and-answer session, explain periodic vs. aperiodic tasks, the background vs. highest-priority dilemma, the EDF utilization advantage, and how IPE combines the DPE mechanism with offline-precomputed EDL idle times.
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude guided the topic with one question at a time. For each step I provided my own understanding (including an exam-routine analogy for offline precomputation), and Claude structured my answers into the Problem Statement / Motivation and Core Technical Contribution sections. The technical content was based on Buttazzo, Chapter 6.

actions: Cross-checked the explanations against the primary reference, Buttazzo, Hard Real-Time Computing Systems, Chapter 6 (Dynamic Priority Servers).

issues: Explanations were simplified for understanding; full mathematical proofs from the book were not reproduced.

integration.section: Section 1 (Problem Statement and Motivation) and Section 2 (Core Technical Contribution)

entries.reflection: The guided question-and-answer process helped me build my own understanding of why IPE exists and how it works. The ideas and the exam-routine analogy came from me; the AI helped phrase and structure them. I verified the technical claims against the textbook before accepting them.

entries.objective: Understand the formal definition of the IPE server: the availability function, the EDL idle-time property, the E and D arrays, the hyperperiod, the replenishment rule, and the schedulability condition.
entries.prompt: Explain the formal definition of IPE step by step: the availability function omega(t), total idle time, why EDL gives the maximum early idle time, the E and D arrays over the hyperperiod, the IPE replenishment rules, and the schedulability condition Up <= 1.
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude explained each formal element with simple examples (for instance, omega(t) = 0 when the CPU is busy, and lcm examples for the hyperperiod). I answered short check-questions to confirm understanding, and the equations and rules were taken from Buttazzo, Chapter 6.

actions: Checked the equations, the definition of the E and D arrays, and the schedulability condition Up <= 1 against Buttazzo, Chapter 6.

issues: The detailed derivation of the EDL idle-time computation was not reproduced; only the result was used.

integration.section: Section 3 (Formal Definition) and Section 4 (Algorithm and Exchange/Replenishment Rules)

entries.reflection: This helped me understand the math behind IPE, especially why Up <= 1 is necessary (the CPU cannot do more than 100% of work) and how the precomputed E and D arrays drive the replenishments. I confirmed the formal statements against the textbook.

entries.objective: Get a quick answer for the spare-time reclaiming rule (what happens when a periodic task finishes earlier than its worst-case execution time).
entries.prompt: What happens to the leftover time when a periodic task finishes earlier than its worst-case execution time, in the context of an EDF aperiodic server?
entries.ai_output_summary: ChatGPT produced an explanation of spare-time reclaiming. I decided not to use its text.

actions: Compared the answer with my own earlier reasoning and the textbook concept of spare-time reclaiming.

issues: I had already reasoned out this point myself (a 10-unit task finishing in 5 units leaves 5 units for aperiodic use), so I used my own explanation instead of the AI text.

entries.reflection: I chose to keep my own understanding rather than copy the AI answer, in line with the requirement that the ideas should be my own.
